where we have used δi=Δi/(vi​Λ)\delta_{i}=\Delta_{i}/(v_{i}\Lambda). We usually deal with the case that δi≪1\delta_{i}\ll 1, so the above equations become (setting α​Λ=1\alpha\Lambda=1)

δ12\displaystyle\delta_{1}^{2} =4​K1π​v1​|δ1|K1​(|g2|​|δ3|K3+|g3|​|δ2|K2),\displaystyle=\frac{4K_{1}}{\pi v_{1}}|\delta_{1}|^{K_{1}}\left(|g_{2}||\delta_{3}|^{K_{3}}+|g_{3}||\delta_{2}|^{K_{2}}\right), (S115)
δ22\displaystyle\delta_{2}^{2} =4​K2π​v2​|δ2|K2​(|g1|​|δ3|K3+|g3|​|δ1|K1),\displaystyle=\frac{4K_{2}}{\pi v_{2}}|\delta_{2}|^{K_{2}}\left(|g_{1}||\delta_{3}|^{K_{3}}+|g_{3}||\delta_{1}|^{K_{1}}\right),
δ32\displaystyle\delta_{3}^{2} =4​K3π​v3​|δ3|K3​(|g2|​|δ1|K1+|g1|​|δ2|K2).\displaystyle=\frac{4K_{3}}{\pi v_{3}}|\delta_{3}|^{K_{3}}\left(|g_{2}||\delta_{1}|^{K_{1}}+|g_{1}||\delta_{2}|^{K_{2}}\right).

It is apparent from these equations that Δi=0\Delta_{i}=0 is always a trivial solution.

The cases with frustration, i.e. when sgn⁡(g1​g2​g3)<0\sgn(g_{1}g_{2}g_{3})<0, are more involved, due to the possible presence of classically degenerate ground states. For instance, in the case when g1=g2=g3<0g_{1}=g_{2}=g_{3}<0, there exist several lines in the parameter space which correspond to the degenerate classical ground state. However, as we see from the RG analysis, this accidental symmetric case g1=g2=g3g_{1}=g_{2}=g_{3} is not protected by any symmetry and is unstable, so we generally do not expect that they are all equal. Therefore, without loss of generality, we assume |g1|>|g2|>|g3||g_{1}|>|g_{2}|>|g_{3}|. In this case, the classical ground state is unique. For instance, when all g1,2,3<0g_{1,2,3}<0, the classical ground state is ϕ1,2=0\phi_{1,2}=0 and ϕ3=±π/2\phi_{3}=\pm\pi/2. After shifting ϕ3\phi_{3} by ±π/2\pm\pi/2 we can still average every field around 00. The derivation of the gap equations is parallel to outlined above, with the only difference being the replacement of |g3||g_{3}| with −|g3|-|g_{3}|. Therefore, we obtain the gap equations for the case with frustration

δ12\displaystyle\delta_{1}^{2} =4​K1π​v1​|δ1|K1​(|g2|​|δ3|K3−|g3|​|δ2|K2),\displaystyle=\frac{4K_{1}}{\pi v_{1}}|\delta_{1}|^{K_{1}}\left(|g_{2}||\delta_{3}|^{K_{3}}-|g_{3}||\delta_{2}|^{K_{2}}\right), (S116)
δ22\displaystyle\delta_{2}^{2} =4​K2π​v2​|δ2|K2​(|g1|​|δ3|K3−|g3|​|δ1|K1),\displaystyle=\frac{4K_{2}}{\pi v_{2}}|\delta_{2}|^{K_{2}}\left(|g_{1}||\delta_{3}|^{K_{3}}-|g_{3}||\delta_{1}|^{K_{1}}\right),
δ32\displaystyle\delta_{3}^{2} =4​K3π​v3​|δ3|K3​(|g2|​|δ1|K1+|g1|​|δ2|K2).\displaystyle=\frac{4K_{3}}{\pi v_{3}}|\delta_{3}|^{K_{3}}\left(|g_{2}||\delta_{1}|^{K_{1}}+|g_{1}||\delta_{2}|^{K_{2}}\right).

In Fig.(S8), we shown the comparison between the solutions of Eq.(S115) and Eq.(S116). We choose the parameters v1,2,3=vv_{1,2,3}=v, g1=0.3​vg_{1}=0.3v, g2=0.25​vg_{2}=0.25v, K1−0.2=K3−0.1=K2=KK_{1}-0.2=K_{3}-0.1=K_{2}=K such that in the case without frustration all induced gaps are comparable. We clearly see from the middle and right panels of Fig.(S8) that in the presence of frustration, all gaps get suppressed compared to the case without frustration. Δ1\Delta_{1} gets suppressed the most and when |g3||g_{3}| gets as large as 0.2​v0.2v, it becomes much smaller than the other two and therefore a gap hierarchy develops.

VI VI. Transport properties

We first show if only the CDW order is considered in the inter-wire coupling, there is no transverse current. To see this, we note the inter-wire coupling Hamiltonian for CDW order is

Hc\displaystyle H_{c} =J​∑⟨i​j⟩∫d​x​OCDW†​(i,x)​OCDW​(j,x)+h.c.\displaystyle=J\sum_{\braket{ij}}\int dxO_{\text{CDW}}^{\dagger}(i,x)O_{\text{CDW}}(j,x)+\text{h.c.} (S117)
=J​∑⟨i​j⟩,λ​λ′∫d​x​ψi,−,λ†​(x)​ψi,+,λ​(x)​ψj,+,λ′†​(x)​ψj,−,λ′​(x)+(i↔j).\displaystyle=J\sum_{\braket{ij},\lambda\lambda^{\prime}}\int dx\psi^{\dagger}_{i,-,\lambda}(x)\psi_{i,+,\lambda}(x)\psi^{\dagger}_{j,+,\lambda^{\prime}}(x)\psi_{j,-,\lambda^{\prime}}(x)+(i\leftrightarrow j).

which is the most relevant one when the system is in the massive phase with gaps in all ϕ2,ϕ3,ϕ4\phi_{2},\phi_{3},\phi_{4} sectors and in the presence of strong repulsion. From this Hamiltonian, one can calculate the current density operator from the continuity equation ∂yjy=i⁡[ρ⁡(i,x),Hc]=0\partial_{y}j_{y}=i[\rho(i,x),H_{c}]=0 and find the current vanishes. Note the vanishing is local, i.e. it’s not because two current operators on ii and jj cancel each other, but rather the current on each wire vanishes. Therefore, we see that by only turning on the CDW coupling is not enough for obtaining a finite cross-wire conductivity, we must have other couplings.

The most trivial one, will be the single particle tunneling (keeping only the nearest neighbor),

Ht=t⊥​∑i,r​r′,λ∫d​x​ψr,λ†​(i,x)​ψr′,λ​(i+1,x)+h.c.H_{t}=t_{\bot}\sum_{i,rr^{\prime},\lambda}\int dx\psi_{r,\lambda}^{\dagger}(i,x)\psi_{r^{\prime},\lambda}(i+1,x)+\text{h.c.} (S118)

The tunneling charge current due to the presence of this Hamiltonian is given by the continuity equation, and we obtain

jy​(i,x)\displaystyle j_{y}(i,x) =i​c​t⊥​∑r,λ(ψr,λ†​(i,x)​ψr,λ​(i+1,x)−ψr,λ†​(i+1,x)​ψr,λ​(i,x)),\displaystyle=ict_{\bot}\sum_{r,\lambda}\left(\psi^{\dagger}_{r,\lambda}(i,x)\psi_{r,\lambda}(i+1,x)-\psi^{\dagger}_{r,\lambda}(i+1,x)\psi_{r,\lambda}(i,x)\right), (S119)
jy​(qy,x)\displaystyle j_{y}(q_{y},x) =−2ct⊥∑r,λ∫−ππdkyψ†r,λ(ky−qy2,x)ψr,λ(ky+qy2,x)sinkyei​qy2,\displaystyle=-2ct_{\bot}\sum_{r,\lambda}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}dk_{y}\psi^{\dagger}_{r,\lambda}(k_{y}-\frac{q_{y}}{2},x)\psi_{r,\lambda}(k_{y}+\frac{q_{y}}{2},x)\sin k_{y}e^{i\frac{q_{y}}{2}},

where cc is the spacing between adjacent wires, and since jy​(i,x)j_{y}(i,x) is Hermitian, jy​(qy,x)†=jy​(−qy,x).j_{y}(q_{y},x)^{\dagger}=j_{y}(-q_{y},x). Below, we will evaluate the current-current correlation in the Hamiltonian without HtH_{t}, similar to the approach in Ref.[13]. However, we will keep HcH_{c} to the first order as in a perturbation theory. According to Kubo formula, the real part of conductivity is given by

Re​σ⊥​(ω)=−e2ω​Im​[limqy→0∫d​x​Π⊥R​(qy,x,ω)]\text{Re}\sigma_{\bot}(\omega)=-\frac{e^{2}}{\omega}\text{Im}\left[\lim_{q_{y}\to 0}\int dx\Pi_{\bot}^{R}(q_{y},x,\omega)\right] (S120)

where Π⊥R​(qy,x,ω)\Pi_{\bot}^{R}(q_{y},x,\omega) is the Fourier transform of the retarded current-current correlation function, which can be obtained from

Π⊥​(qy,x,i​ωn)=⟨jy​(qy,x,i​ωn)​jy​(−qy,0,−i​ωn)⟩\Pi_{\bot}(q_{y},x,i\omega_{n})=\braket{j_{y}(q_{y},x,i\omega_{n})j_{y}(-q_{y},0,-i\omega_{n})} (S121)

by analytic continuation. Here we have assumed translation symmetry. To the first order in HcH_{c}, we have

limqy→0∫d​x​Π⊥​(qy,x,i​ωn)=1β​∑i​kn∑r,λ∫d​kx​d​ky(2​π)2​4​c2​t⊥2​sin2⁡ky​Gr,λ​(kx,i​kn)​Gr,λ​(kx,i​kn+i​ωn)\displaystyle\lim_{q_{y}\to 0}\int dx\Pi_{\bot}(q_{y},x,i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{ik_{n}}\sum_{r,\lambda}\int\frac{dk_{x}dk_{y}}{(2\pi)^{2}}4c^{2}t_{\bot}^{2}\sin^{2}k_{y}G_{r,\lambda}(k_{x},ik_{n})G_{r,\lambda}(k_{x},ik_{n}+i\omega_{n}) (S122)
+\displaystyle+ Jβ2​∑i​kn,i​pn∑r,λ∫d2​𝒌​d2​𝒑(2​π)4​4​c2​t⊥2​sin2⁡ky​sin2⁡py​Gr,λ​(kx,i​kn)​Gr,λ​(kx,i​kn+i​ωn)​G−r,λ​(px,i​pn)​G−r,λ​(px,i​pn+i​ωn).\displaystyle\frac{J}{\beta^{2}}\sum_{ik_{n},ip_{n}}\sum_{r,\lambda}\int\frac{d^{2}\bm{k}d^{2}\bm{p}}{(2\pi)^{4}}4c^{2}t_{\bot}^{2}\sin^{2}k_{y}\sin^{2}p_{y}G_{r,\lambda}(k_{x},ik_{n})G_{r,\lambda}(k_{x},ik_{n}+i\omega_{n})G_{-r,\lambda}(p_{x},ip_{n})G_{-r,\lambda}(p_{x},ip_{n}+i\omega_{n}).

Here we used the fact that all the Green’s functions are evaluated in the decoupled Hamiltonian, so these are essentially 1D Hamiltonians and do not depend on kyk_{y} or the wire index. Note in the second line of Eq.(S122) the difference in the rr-index between these Green’s functions are due to the nature of the CDW interaction HcH_{c}. Upon expressing the Green’s functions using their spectral representations

G⁡(kx,i​kn)=12​π​∫d​ε​A⁡(kx,ε)i​kn−ε,A⁡(kx,ε)=−2​Im​GR​(kx,ε)G(k_{x},ik_{n})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int d\varepsilon\frac{A(k_{x},\varepsilon)}{ik_{n}-\varepsilon},~~A(k_{x},\varepsilon)=-2\text{Im}G^{R}(k_{x},\varepsilon) (S123)

and analytically continuing on the real frequency axis by changing i​ωni\omega_{n} to ω+i​0+\omega+i0^{+}, we obtain (after summing over i​knik_{n})

Re​σ⊥​(ω)=e2​c​t⊥22​π​∑r,λ∫d​x​∫d​ε​nF​(ε)−nF​(ε+ω)ω​Ar,λ​(x,ε)​Ar,λ​(−x,ε+ω)\displaystyle\text{Re}\sigma_{\bot}(\omega)=\frac{e^{2}ct_{\bot}^{2}}{2\pi}\sum_{r,\lambda}\int dx\int d\varepsilon\frac{n_{F}(\varepsilon)-n_{F}(\varepsilon+\omega)}{\omega}A_{r,\lambda}(x,\varepsilon)A_{r,\lambda}(-x,\varepsilon+\omega) (S124)
+e2​J​t⊥28​π3∑r,λ∫dxdx′P∫dϵdϵ′nF​(ϵ)−nF​(ϵ′)ω+ϵ−ϵ′Ar,λ(x,ϵ)Ar,λ(−x,ϵ′)∫dεnF​(ε)−nF​(ε+ω)ωA−r,λ(x′,ε)A−r,λ(−x′,ε+ω),\displaystyle+\frac{e^{2}Jt_{\bot}^{2}}{8\pi^{3}}\sum_{r,\lambda}\int dxdx^{\prime}P\int d\epsilon d\epsilon^{\prime}\frac{n_{F}(\epsilon)-n_{F}(\epsilon^{\prime})}{\omega+\epsilon-\epsilon^{\prime}}A_{r,\lambda}(x,\epsilon)A_{r,\lambda}(-x,\epsilon^{\prime})\int d\varepsilon\frac{n_{F}(\varepsilon)-n_{F}(\varepsilon+\omega)}{\omega}A_{-r,\lambda}(x^{\prime},\varepsilon)A_{-r,\lambda}(-x^{\prime},\varepsilon+\omega),

where in the second line we use P∫P\int to denote the principle value integral. To proceed with obtaining the temperature , we need the spectral function for the decoupled 1D system. But here we can estimate the magnitude of σ⊥\sigma_{\bot} from the its prefactors (after restoring ℏ\hbar everywhere),

σ⊥​(T)=e2h​4​(a​c​kF2)​(t⊥EF)2​F​(TEF)≈18​e2h​(t⊥EF)2​F​(TEF)​for​kF≈π2​a\sigma_{\bot}(T)=\frac{e^{2}}{h}4(ack_{F}^{2})\left(\frac{t_{\bot}}{E_{F}}\right)^{2}F\left(\frac{T}{E_{F}}\right)\approx 18\frac{e^{2}}{h}\left(\frac{t_{\bot}}{E_{F}}\right)^{2}F\left(\frac{T}{E_{F}}\right)~~\text{for}~~k_{F}\approx\frac{\pi}{2a} (S125)

where FF is some dimensionless function that comes from the integral involving the spectral functions.

VI.1 A. Single-particle tunneling in the gapless case

We begin by discussing the conductivity due to the single particle tunneling process in the gapless case, i.e. all the four ϕj\phi_{j} fields are gapless. As shown above, this requires the calculation of the single particle spectral function. By definition, the retarded single particle Green’s function is given by

Gr,λR​(x,t)=−i​Θ​(t)​⟨{ψr,λ​(x,t),ψr,λ†​(0,0)}⟩=−i​Θ​(t)​(Gr,λ​(x,t)+Gr,λ​(−x,−t))G^{R}_{r,\lambda}(x,t)=-i\Theta(t)\braket{\{\psi_{r,\lambda}(x,t),\psi^{\dagger}_{r,\lambda}(0,0)\}}=-i\Theta(t)(G_{r,\lambda}(x,t)+G_{r,\lambda}(-x,-t)) (S126)

where

Gr,λ​(x,t)=limα→0ei​r​kF​x2​π​α​⟨ei​θλ​(x,t)−i​r​ϕλ​(x,t)​e−i​θλ​(0,0)+i​r​ϕλ​(0,0)⟩G_{r,\lambda}(x,t)=\lim_{\alpha\to 0}\frac{e^{irk_{F}x}}{2\pi\alpha}\braket{e^{i\theta_{\lambda}(x,t)-ir\phi_{\lambda}(x,t)}e^{-i\theta_{\lambda}(0,0)+ir\phi_{\lambda}(0,0)}} (S127)

according to Eq.(S21). Without loss of generality, we take r=+r=+ and λ=↑u\lambda=\uparrow u. Using Eq.(S23) we have

Gr,λ​(x,t)=limα→0ei​r​kF​x2​π​α​∏j=03⟨ei2​[θj​(x,t)−ϕj​(x,t)]​e−i2​[θj​(0,0)−ϕj​(0,0)]⟩jG_{r,\lambda}(x,t)=\lim_{\alpha\to 0}\frac{e^{irk_{F}x}}{2\pi\alpha}\prod_{j=0}^{3}\braket{e^{\frac{i}{2}[\theta_{j}(x,t)-\phi_{j}(x,t)]}e^{-\frac{i}{2}[\theta_{j}(0,0)-\phi_{j}(0,0)]}}_{j} (S128)

For Gaussian models we have ⟨ei​A​e−i​B⟩=exp⁡(−12​⟨A2⟩−12​⟨B2⟩+⟨A​B⟩)\braket{e^{iA}e^{-iB}}=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\braket{A^{2}}-\frac{1}{2}\braket{B^{2}}+\braket{AB}\right), thus

⟨ei2​[θj​(x,t)−ϕj​(x,t)]​e−i2​[θj​(0,0)−ϕj​(0,0)]⟩j=exp⁡[14​⟨(θj​(x,t)−ϕj​(x,t))​(θj​(0,0)−ϕj​(0,0))⟩j−14​⟨(θj−ϕj)2⟩j].\braket{e^{\frac{i}{2}[\theta_{j}(x,t)-\phi_{j}(x,t)]}e^{-\frac{i}{2}[\theta_{j}(0,0)-\phi_{j}(0,0)]}}_{j}=\exp\left[\frac{1}{4}\braket{\left(\theta_{j}(x,t)-\phi_{j}(x,t)\right)\left(\theta_{j}(0,0)-\phi_{j}(0,0)\right)}_{j}-\frac{1}{4}\braket{(\theta_{j}-\phi_{j})^{2}}_{j}\right]. (S129)

Using Eq.(S42), (S43) and (S44), it is easy to see

⟨ei2​[θj​(x,t)−ϕj​(x,t)]​e−i2​[θj​(0,0)−ϕj​(0,0)]⟩j=(aa+i⁡(vj​t−x))1/4​(a2x2+(i​vj​t+a)2)Kj+1Kj−216.\braket{e^{\frac{i}{2}[\theta_{j}(x,t)-\phi_{j}(x,t)]}e^{-\frac{i}{2}[\theta_{j}(0,0)-\phi_{j}(0,0)]}}_{j}=\left(\frac{a}{a+i(v_{j}t-x)}\right)^{1/4}\left(\frac{a^{2}}{x^{2}+(iv_{j}t+a)^{2}}\right)^{\frac{K_{j}+\frac{1}{K_{j}}-2}{16}}. (S130)

As a result, we have,

G+,↑A​(x,t)=ei​kF​x2​π​∏j=03(1a+i⁡(vj​t−x))1/4​(a2x2+(i​vj​t+a)2)γj/2,γj=Kj+1Kj−28G_{+,\uparrow A}(x,t)=\frac{e^{ik_{F}x}}{2\pi}\prod_{j=0}^{3}\left(\frac{1}{a+i(v_{j}t-x)}\right)^{1/4}\left(\frac{a^{2}}{x^{2}+(iv_{j}t+a)^{2}}\right)^{\gamma_{j}/2},~~~\gamma_{j}=\frac{K_{j}+\frac{1}{K_{j}}-2}{8} (S131)

In fact, this form does not depend on λ\lambda. For r=−r=-, the only changes is to replace xx with −x-x in the above expression.

For comparison, we note in the conventional two-component case, we have

G⁡(x,t)∼∏j=c,s(1a+i⁡(vj​t−x))1/2​(a2x2+(i​vj​t+a)2)γj/2,γj=Kj+1Kj−24.G(x,t)\sim\prod_{j=c,s}\left(\frac{1}{a+i(v_{j}t-x)}\right)^{1/2}\left(\frac{a^{2}}{x^{2}+(iv_{j}t+a)^{2}}\right)^{\gamma_{j}/2},~~~\gamma_{j}=\frac{K_{j}+\frac{1}{K_{j}}-2}{4}. (S132)

Using this result, and if we neglect the correction due to the CDW order coupling, we have

Reσ⊥(ω→0,T)\displaystyle\text{Re}\sigma_{\bot}(\omega\to 0,T) ∼∫d​x​∫d​ε​14​T​sech2​(ε2​T)​A​(x,ε)​A​(−x,ε+ω)\displaystyle\sim\int dx\int d\varepsilon\frac{1}{4T}\text{sech}^{2}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2T}\right)A(x,\varepsilon)A(-x,\varepsilon+\omega) (S133)
∼∫d​x​∫d​ε​14​T​sech2​(ε2​T)​F​(x,ε)\displaystyle\sim\int dx\int d\varepsilon\frac{1}{4T}\text{sech}^{2}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2T}\right)F(x,\varepsilon)

where F⁡(x,ε)F(x,\varepsilon) obeys

F⁡(a​x,εa)=1a2​γ​F​(x,ε),γ=∑jγj.F\left(ax,\frac{\varepsilon}{a}\right)=\frac{1}{a^{2\gamma}}F(x,\varepsilon),~~~\gamma=\sum_{j}\gamma_{j}. (S134)

The spectral function A⁡(x,ε)A(x,\varepsilon) has the following properties:

A⁡(x=0,ε)=N⁡(ε)∼|ε|γ,A⁡(x≫1/ε,ε)∼cos⁡ε​xxγ,A(x=0,\varepsilon)=N(\varepsilon)\sim|\varepsilon|^{\gamma},~~~A(x\gg 1/\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\sim\frac{\cos{\varepsilon x}}{x^{\gamma}}, (S135)

so the function F⁡(x,ε)F(x,\varepsilon) behaves like

F⁡(x,ε)\displaystyle F(x,\varepsilon) ∼ε2​γ​for​x≪1/ε,\displaystyle\sim\varepsilon^{2\gamma}~\text{for}~x\ll 1/\varepsilon, (S136)
∼1x2​γ​for​x≫1/ε.\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{x^{2\gamma}}~\text{for}~x\gg 1/\varepsilon.

Therefore

Reσ⊥(ω→0,T)∼∫dε14​Tsech2(ε2​T)(∫01/εdxε2​γ+∫1/ε+∞dxcos⁡2​ε​xx2​γ)∼T2​γ−1.\text{Re}\sigma_{\bot}(\omega\to 0,T)\sim\int d\varepsilon\frac{1}{4T}\text{sech}^{2}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2T}\right)\left(\int_{0}^{1/\varepsilon}dx\varepsilon^{2\gamma}+\int_{1/\varepsilon}^{+\infty}dx\frac{\cos{2\varepsilon x}}{x^{2\gamma}}\right)\sim T^{2\gamma-1}. (S137)

In the main text, we introduce the scaling dimension of the single particle hopping αe\alpha_{e}, which is related to γ\gamma simply by γ=αe−1\gamma=\alpha_{e}-1.

VI.2 B. Single-particle tunneling in the gapped case

When there is a gap opening in either one or more of the ϕj\phi_{j} fields, the total single particle density of states has a gap structure. This is because the total real pace Green’s function is a product of the four component, as shown in Eq.(S131). Consequently, the spectral function (and hence the density of states), which is the Fourier transform of Eq.(S131), is a convolution of different components. It is this convolution that leads to a gap in the total spectral function. For two component 1DEG this was demonstrated in Ref.[12] If there is a gap in the total density of states, the conductivity becomes zero when TT is below the gap energy scale. However, when TT is well above the energy scale set by the gap, Eq.(S137) still applies.

VI.3 C. Josephson tunneling in the gapped case

Unlike the single particle tunneling, the pair or quadruple hopping process does not depend on the single particle density of states, and can contribute to the cross wire conductivity even in the gapped phase and when TT not well above the gap energy scale. Below we discuss this Josephson tunneling due to charge-2e and charge-4e orders.

VI.3.1 1. charge-2e superconductivity

We take spin-triplet pseudospin-triplet pairing order parameter in Eq.(S64) as an example. Assuming we are in the partially gapped phase when ϕ2,3\phi_{2,3} are gapped. The tunneling is governed by the Hamiltonian

HJ\displaystyle H_{J} =Js​∑⟨y,y′⟩∫d​x​OT1,S†​(x,y)​OT1,S​(x,y′)+h.c.\displaystyle=J_{s}\sum_{\braket{y,y^{\prime}}}\int dxO_{T_{1},S}^{\dagger}(x,y)O_{T_{1},S}(x,y^{\prime})+\text{h.c.} (S138)
=J~s​∑⟨y,y′⟩∫d​x​cos⁡[θ0​(x,y)+θ1​(x,y)−θ0​(x,y′)−θ1​(x,y′)],\displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{s}\sum_{\braket{y,y^{\prime}}}\int dx\cos\left[\theta_{0}(x,y)+\theta_{1}(x,y)-\theta_{0}(x,y^{\prime})-\theta_{1}(x,y^{\prime})\right],

where J~s=Js​δ2K2/2​δ3K3/2\tilde{J}_{s}=J_{s}\delta_{2}^{K_{2}/2}\delta_{3}^{K_{3}/2} and Js∼t⊥2/EFJ_{s}\sim t_{\bot}^{2}/E_{F}. On the other hand, the local charge density operator is given by ρ0​(x,y)=1π​∂xϕ0​(x,y)\rho_{0}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\pi}\partial_{x}\phi_{0}(x,y). Then according to the continuity equation, the transverse current density is found to be

jy​(x)=J~s​c​sin⁡[θ0​(x,y+1)+θ1​(x,y+1)−θ0​(x,y)−θ1​(x,y)]j_{y}(x)=\tilde{J}_{s}c\sin[\theta_{0}(x,y+1)+\theta_{1}(x,y+1)-\theta_{0}(x,y)-\theta_{1}(x,y)] (S139)

which is the Josephson current. To evaluate the current-current correlation in the decoupled 1D system, we note that only the correlation involving two current operators with the same yy survives. Thus we have

Π⊥​(x,y,τ)\displaystyle\Pi_{\bot}(x,y,\tau) =J~s2​c2​⟨sin⁡[θ0​(x,y+1)+θ1​(x,y+1)−θ0​(x,y)−θ1​(x,y)]​sin⁡[θ0​(0,0+1)+θ1​(0,0+1)−θ0​(0,0)−θ1​(0,0)]⟩\displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{s}^{2}c^{2}\braket{\sin[\theta_{0}(x,y+1)+\theta_{1}(x,y+1)-\theta_{0}(x,y)-\theta_{1}(x,y)]\sin[\theta_{0}(0,0+1)+\theta_{1}(0,0+1)-\theta_{0}(0,0)-\theta_{1}(0,0)]} (S140)
=J~s2​c22​(a2x2+v02​τ2+a2)12​K0+12​K1​δy,0.\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{J}_{s}^{2}c^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{a^{2}}{x^{2}+v_{0}^{2}\tau^{2}+a^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2K_{0}}+\frac{1}{2K_{1}}}\delta_{y,0}.

Therefore

Π⊥(𝒒→0,ω)=∫dxdtei​ω​t∑yΠ⊥(x,y,t)∼J~s2c2ω1/K0+1/K1−2\Pi_{\bot}(\bm{q}\to 0,\omega)=\int dxdte^{i\omega t}\sum_{y}\Pi_{\bot}(x,y,t)\sim\tilde{J}_{s}^{2}c^{2}\omega^{1/K_{0}+1/K_{1}-2} (S141)

and

Re​σ​(ω)∼J~s2​c2​ω1/K0+1/K1−3→Re​σ​(T)∼J~s2​c2​T1/K0+1/K1−3.\text{Re}\sigma(\omega)\sim\tilde{J}_{s}^{2}c^{2}\omega^{1/K_{0}+1/K_{1}-3}\to\text{Re}\sigma(T)\sim\tilde{J}_{s}^{2}c^{2}T^{1/K_{0}+1/K_{1}-3}. (S142)

VI.3.2 2. charge-4e superconductivity

Like the charge-2e superconductivity case, the tunneling current is determined by the coupling Hamiltonian,

HJ\displaystyle H_{J} =J~s​∑⟨y,y′⟩∫d​x​cos⁡[2​θ0​(x,y)−2​θ0​(x,y′)].\displaystyle=\tilde{J}_{s}\sum_{\braket{y,y^{\prime}}}\int dx\cos\left[2\theta_{0}(x,y)-2\theta_{0}(x,y^{\prime})\right]. (S143)

The resulting current operator is

jy​(x)=J~s​c​sin⁡[2​θ0​(x,y+1)−2​θ0​(x,y)].j_{y}(x)=\tilde{J}_{s}c\sin[2\theta_{0}(x,y+1)-2\theta_{0}(x,y)]. (S144)

The calculation of conductivity is exactly the same as the 2e-SC case, with the modification of θ0→2​θ0\theta_{0}\to 2\theta_{0} and hence 1/K0→4/K01/K_{0}\to 4/K_{0}, and the final result is

Re​σ​(T)∼J~s2​c2​T4/K0−3\text{Re}\sigma(T)\sim\tilde{J}_{s}^{2}c^{2}T^{4/K_{0}-3} (S145)
